title: Brief interpersonal therapy reduces anxiety during pregnancy: A randomized clinical trial.
authors: Demers CH, Curci SG, Hennessey EP, Gallop RJ, Hoffman MC, Grote NK, Hankin BL, Davis EP
abstract: Anxiety disorders are highly prevalent during pregnancy and are associated with negative maternal and infant health outcomes. However, research has focused on perinatal depression, leaving critical gaps in evidence for effective anxiety interventions. Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT), well-established for treating perinatal depression, remains understudied. The current study examined anxiety outcomes from the Care Project, a randomized controlled trial that evaluated brief IPT (MOMCare) compared with Enhanced Usual Care (EUC) for prenatal depression. Participants included 234 distressed pregnant individuals, randomized to IPT (n = 115) or EUC (n = 119). Anxiety symptoms were assessed using the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory across gestation. Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) was assessed at the end of pregnancy via the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5. Anxiety symptoms declined significantly across pregnancy in both groups (F(1,229) = 54.87, P < .0001). The overall treatment-by-time interaction did not reach conventional statistical significance (t(229) = 1.84, P = .067). Participants receiving IPT had significantly lower anxiety levels relative to participants in EUC beginning 8 weeks after randomization (~24 weeks' gestational age; t(229) = 2.14, P = .03, d = 0.28). By the end of pregnancy, anxiety symptoms were on average 5.2 points lower among IPT relative to EUC participants (t(229) = 2.62, P = .009, d = 0.35). GAD prevalence declined from baseline to the end of pregnancy in both groups (IPT: 46.4% decrease to 13.2%; EUC: 47.4% decrease to 16.9%), although groups did not differ in GAD diagnostic status at the end of pregnancy. Findings support IPT's potential for reducing perinatal anxiety symptoms, highlighting the need for research to optimize treatment effectiveness across the perinatal period. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03011801.

title: Prospective Multicenter Evaluation of a Novel Low-Axial-Force Colonic Stent for Malignant Colorectal Obstruction.
authors: Otsuka R, Saito S, Fujimoto N, Hanabata N, Takao A, Narita K, Kuwai T, Endo S
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Self-expandable metal stents (SEMSs) are used as a bridge to surgery (BTS) or for palliation (PAL) in malignant colorectal obstruction, but high axial force may contribute to perforation. We prospectively evaluated the efficacy and safety of the low-axial-force Naturfit colonic stent in both settings. METHODS: This prospective multicenter single-arm study enrolled 208 patients at 11 Japanese institutions between 2019 and 2022 (BTS, n = 137; PAL, n = 71). The primary endpoint was clinical success of colorectal stenting; secondary endpoints included technical success, adverse events, surgical outcomes after BTS stenting, and 12-month palliative outcomes. RESULTS: Technical success and clinical success of colorectal stenting were both 99.0%, with perforation in three patients (1.4%). In the BTS cohort, clinical success of BTS was 97.1%; no perforations occurred, and early and late adverse-event rates were 1.5% and 3.7%. All patients underwent elective surgery; colostomy and laparoscopic surgery rates were 4.4% and 87.6%. In the palliative cohort, clinical success of colorectal stenting was 98.6%, late adverse events occurred in 16.9%, and 12-month overall survival and stent patency were 46.6% and 67.6%. CONCLUSIONS: Naturfit achieved high technical and clinical success of colorectal stenting with a low perforation rate. These findings support its feasibility for malignant colorectal obstruction in both BTS and palliative settings, although comparative studies are needed to determine relative advantages over other SEMSs. TRIAL REGISTRATION: University Hospital Medical Information Network Clinical Trial Registry: UMIN000035224.

title: Depressive symptoms trajectories among adult women in South Korea: A latent class growth analysis using longitudinal panel data.
authors: Yu S, Song IH
abstract: BACKGROUND: Depressive symptom is a leading contributor to disease burden globally, with women disproportionately affected. However, the heterogeneous longitudinal trajectories of depressive symptoms among adult women remain insufficiently examined. This study aimed to identify distinct trajectory classes of depressive symptoms among South Korean adult women and to examine baseline individual-, family-, and community-related characteristics associated with membership in these trajectory classes. METHODS: Data were drawn from Waves 6 through 9 of the Korean Longitudinal Survey of Women and Families (KLoWF), comprising 5513 adult women. Depressive symptoms were measured using the CES-D 10. Latent class growth analysis (LCGA) was applied to identify trajectory classes, and multinomial logistic regression was used to examine factors associated with trajectory class membership based on Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems framework. RESULTS: Three distinct trajectory classes were identified: a stable low depressive symptoms class (78.6%), an elevated but decreasing depressive symptoms class (10.8%), and an increasing depressive symptoms class (10.7%). Stress, pregnancy/childbirth experience, traditional marriage values, employment status, household income, and family violence were significantly associated with membership in distinct trajectory classes. LIMITATIONS: The study relied on four time points and self-report measures. LCGA does not account for within-class variance. CONCLUSIONS: Depressive symptoms trajectories among adult women are heterogeneous, shaped by multi-level ecological risk factors. Findings underscore the need for longitudinal monitoring, integrated mental health and social welfare policies, and trajectory-informed interventions targeting structurally vulnerable subgroups.

title: Next-generation anti-obesity drugs: emerging molecular targets and translational opportunities.
authors: Shetty S, Rangle A, Mukherjee AG, Bharti AK, Jena SP, Prince SE, Gopalakrishnan AV
journal: Journal of diabetes and metabolic disorders
abstract: PURPOSE: Obesity is a heterogeneous, chronic metabolic disease driven by dysregulation of energy homeostasis across interconnected central nervous system, gastrointestinal, adipose, endocrine, immune, and mitochondrial networks. Despite the established roles of lifestyle intervention and metabolic/bariatric surgery, limitations in accessibility, durability, and interindividual response have stimulated the development of mechanism-based pharmacotherapies. This review critically examines emerging therapeutic strategies targeting integrated energy-regulatory pathways and evaluates their translational potential for precision obesity management. METHODS: Current evidence was synthesized across major biological systems governing appetite, energy expenditure, and metabolic adaptation. Central melanocortin, Neuropeptide Y (NPY)/ Agouti-related peptide (AgRP), serotonergic, dopaminergic, and endocannabinoid pathways were considered alongside gut-derived incretin, amylin, Peptide YY (PYY), ghrelin, Fibroblast Growth Factor (FGF), and bile acid signaling. Emerging approaches targeting adipose remodeling, thermogenesis, mitochondrial energetics, AMPK-mTOR-sirtuin signaling, inflammation, and fibrosis were also evaluated. Genetic, epigenetic, and artificial intelligence-based approaches to patient stratification were incorporated to assess prospects for precision therapy. RESULTS: Obesity pharmacotherapy is shifting from conventional appetite suppression toward coordinated modulation of interconnected metabolic pathways. Incretin-based and multi-agonist therapies provide the strongest clinical evidence for substantial weight reduction and metabolic improvement. However, treatment discontinuation, weight regain, adverse effects, cost, and heterogeneous therapeutic responses remain major challenges. Strategies targeting adipose tissue dysfunction, mitochondrial metabolism, thermogenesis, immune-metabolic signaling, and fibrosis offer additional opportunities for disease modification, although many remain in preclinical or early clinical development. Increasing evidence for biological heterogeneity supports individualized therapeutic selection. CONCLUSION: The emerging therapeutic paradigm positions obesity as a systems-level disorder requiring mechanism-informed, individualized intervention. Integrating CNS-gut-adipose-mitochondrial biology with multi-omics, biomarkers, and artificial intelligence may enable more durable and precise treatment. Long-term safety, durability, affordability, equitable access, and clinical validation remain essential for translation.

title: Consent for intensive care research involving adults who lack decision-making capacity: A jurisdictional analysis of Australia's fragmented framework.
authors: Bihari S, Galluccio S, McIntyre J, Plummer M, Nair P, Saxena M, Buhr H, Neto AS
journal: Critical care and resuscitation : journal of the Australasian Academy of Critical Care Medicine
abstract: Critically ill adults frequently cannot consent to research because of sedation, delirium, shock or mechanical ventilation, yet safe intensive care depends on evidence generated in this population; several treatments once regarded as standard care proved harmful when finally tested in randomised trials. The ethical framework for enrolling adults who lack decision-making capacity is national-the National Health and Medical Research Council National Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research (2025), in effect since 23 June 2026-but legal authority for substitute consent is conferred by eight state and territory statutes that differ in terminology, in decision-maker hierarchies, in whether they address research at all, and whether they permit enrolment in an emergency. Mapping four representative study archetypes across all eight jurisdictions shows that the lawful basis for enrolling the same patient shifts with study design as much as with geography; differing statutory definitions, tribunal involvement and the transition to the 2025 National Statement produce material and avoidable inconsistency. Contemporary Australian intensive care trials show that practice has converged on the National Statement while the underlying legislation has not; the resulting inconsistency risks inequity, underrepresentation of critically ill patients, and bias in the evidence generated. We set out principles for reform (Box 1): nationally consistent framing of substitute consent for research-common terminology and legal principles, an explicit emergency-research pathway in every jurisdiction, and consistent interpretation within each jurisdiction-developed with consumers and with the clinicians and clinical research nurses who obtain consent, and taken forward with formal endorsement from the relevant professional bodies.

title: Kidney effects of inhaled nitric oxide in critically ill patients: from pathophysiological considerations to clinical implications.
authors: Robert A, Gonze A, Bulpa P, Hauquiert B
abstract: Inhaled nitric oxide is widely used as a selective pulmonary vasodilator in critical care, yet its renal effects remain controversial. While existing reviews mostly focus on indications for inhaled nitric oxide and its impact on outcomes, limited data exist on its renal effects, since it was thought to act only locally in the lungs. This review examine the clinical evidence regarding kidney outcomes associated with inhaled nitric oxide across major indications and provide an integrated mechanistic analysis of nitric oxide signaling in renal physiology and pathophysiology. Nitric oxide is produced by nitric oxide synthases using L-arginine as a substrate. It acts as a smooth muscle relaxation factor and ultimately causes vasodilation through its effect on cyclic guanosine monophosphate. Nitric oxide plays a pivotal role in renal hemodynamic regulation, glomerular filtration, tubular function, and microcirculatory homeostasis. The net renal effect of inhaled nitric oxide likely reflects the balance between improved nitric oxide signaling and oxidative stress generation. Available clinical data suggest that the renal impact of inhaled nitric oxide is context-dependent. In acute respiratory distress syndrome, higher-level evidence indicates a potential increase in acute kidney injury, possibly related to oxidative and nitrosative stress. Conversely, in cardiac bypass surgery, inhaled nitric oxide may confer nephroprotection by restoring nitric oxide bioavailability during hemolysis and free hemoglobin-mediated nitric oxide scavenging. In other conditions, including organ transplantation, pulmonary hypertension, sepsis, and hemolytic disorders, evidence remains limited or inconclusive. Overall, current evidence does not support a uniform renal effect of inhaled nitric oxide, indicating the need for prospective studies with predefined renal endpoints to clarify its clinical relevance.

title: Serrated Pathway-Related Post-Colonoscopy Colorectal Cancer　Detected During Surveillance Colonoscopy: A Case Report.
authors: Hadatsuki H, Ichijima R, Mizuguchi Y, Toyoshima N, Okita H, Haga T, Kumamoto Y, Tsukamoto S
abstract: Post-colonoscopy colorectal cancer (PCCRC) remains a critical clinical challenge, and sessile serrated lesions (SSLs) are important precursor lesions. We report a case of advanced transverse colon cancer suspected to be associated with the serrated pathway that was detected during periodic surveillance colonoscopy. An 82-year-old male had undergone periodic surveillance colonoscopy after curative resection via endoscopic submucosal dissection for rectosigmoid intramucosal cancer. Colonoscopy revealed a type 2 advanced tumor near the hepatic flexure and multiple serrated lesions throughout the colon, fulfilling the diagnostic criteria for serrated polyposis syndrome (SPS). Immunohistochemistry showed deficient mismatch repair with loss of MLH1 and PMS2, and molecular analysis revealed BRAF V600E and KRAS mutations. The patient underwent robot-assisted transverse colectomy, and pathological staging was pT3N0. He remains recurrence-free 6 months after surgery. This case highlights the difficulty of distinguishing between a missed serrated lesion and a newly developed cancer in serrated pathway-related PCCRC. In patients with multiple SSLs or SPS, high-quality colonoscopy, recognition of SPS criteria, complete resection of detectable serrated lesions, and individualized surveillance strategies may be essential for the prevention and early detection of PCCRC.

title: DksA orchestrates redox-sensitive virulence trade-off between P fimbriae and K1 capsule expression to promote Escherichia coli-induced sepsis.
authors: Zhu D, Shi X, Fu S, Ma W, Huang A, Jiang M, Liang Y, Zhao Y
abstract: Extraintestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli (ExPEC) is a leading cause of life-threatening sepsis worldwide. A key unresolved question in ExPEC pathogenesis is how these strains initiate and drive severe, high-mortality sepsis. RNA polymerase (RNAP)-binding transcriptional regulator DksA is known to mediate bacterial stress responses. Here, we demonstrate that DksA acts as a critical regulator of ExPEC-induced sepsis. DksA functions as a redox-sensitive molecular switch that modulates virulence trade-off between P fimbriae-mediated adhesion and K1 capsule-dependent immune evasion via the novel sRNA PRs37 (originally designated sRNA037), directly repressing the major pilin subunit PapA. DksA binds RNAP to repress transcription of PRs37 and K1 capsule operons. Oxidative stress triggered by oxidants such as H₂O₂ induces cysteine oxidation of DksA, relieving its transcriptional repression and enhancing ExPEC immune evasion. This DksA redox-dependent regulation operates independently of molecular chaperones and the stringent response. This DksA-orchestrated virulence trade-off serves as a key determinant for the establishment and progression of E. coli sepsis. Our findings deepen the understanding of complex host-pathogen interactions and provide a theoretical foundation for developing novel anti-infective strategies.

title: Time to treatment of critical hypertension within 30 minutes and obstetrical outcomes.
authors: Kobara E, Miller E, Rajesh R, Vertichio R, Akerman M, Prasannan L, Suhag A
journal: The journal of maternal-fetal & neonatal medicine : the official journal of the European Association of Perinatal Medicine, the Federation of Asia and Oceania Perinatal Societies, the International Society of Perinatal Obstetricians
abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate whether treatment of critical hypertension within 30 min, compared to treatment greater than or equal to 30 min, is associated with lower severe maternal morbidity (SMM). STUDY DESIGN: This retrospective cohort study analyzed pregnant patients with singleton gestations ≥20 weeks with critical hypertension [defined as persistent HTN with 2 consecutive SBP ≥160 or DBP ≥110 mm HG at least 15 min apart], who delivered between January 2021 and December 2022 at a single tertiary care center. Time to treatment was measured from the confirmatory second blood pressure reading to the time of antihypertensive administration. The study compared Group A (treatment time <30 min) with Group B (treatment time ≥30 min). The primary outcome was composite SMM, and secondary outcomes included composite severe neonatal morbidity (SNM), preterm birth, placental abruption, non-reassuring fetal heart tracing (NRFHT), and postpartum readmission. Multivariable logistic regression was adjusted for a set of baseline confounders. Statistical significance was set as p < 0.05. RESULTS: Out of 370 patients screened, 271 met inclusion criteria (214 in Group A and 57 in Group B). Median time to treatment was 11 min (IQR 6-17) in Group A and 47 min (IQR 38-194) in Group B. Compared with Group B, patients in Group A were younger and had higher admission systolic and diastolic blood pressures. SMM occurred in 27 (12.6%) patients in Group A and 11 (19.3%) in Group B (unadjusted odds ratio [OR] for Group B vs. Group A 1.66, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.77-3.58; adjusted OR 1.77, 95% CI 0.80-3.91). SNM occurred in 56 (26.2%) and 14 (24.6%) patients, respectively (unadjusted OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.47-1.81). Results were consistent across sensitivity analyses, and no secondary outcome differed significantly between groups. CONCLUSION: In this single-center retrospective cohort, we did not detect a statistically significant difference in SMM between patients treated within 30 min and those treated later. The confidence intervals were wide and do not exclude a clinically important benefit of earlier treatment, and these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence. Treatment of acute-onset severe hypertension as soon as reasonably possible should remain the standard, and adequately powered prospective studies, including randomized trials, are needed to define the optimal treatment interval.

title: Young children engage in choice-relative moral reasoning.
authors: Waltzer T, Heyman GD, Leslie AM, Levine S
abstract: A central challenge in moral reasoning is evaluating actions not only by their outcomes, but also by the alternatives that were available at the time of choice. The present study examined whether preschool-age children engage in this form of choice-relative moral reasoning. Using a child-friendly version of the trolley problem, 3- to 5-year-old children (N = 124, 51% girls) judged a protagonist who moved a barrier to protect three children's cookies from being eaten by a mean squirrel. Children typically judged this action as morally good when no better alternative was available, even when it caused harm to another child. However, they judged the same action as morally bad when a non-harmful alternative was available but not chosen. These findings suggest that preschool-age children evaluate actions in light of available alternatives rather than solely on the basis of outcomes. Thus, even young children appear to consider what else could have been done when making moral judgments.

title: Do parental questions and gestures support executive functions in toddlers born preterm and full-term?
authors: Yılmaz B, Göksun T
abstract: This study examined parental questions and gestures in the development of executive functions (EF) in preterm (PT) and full-term (FT) toddlers. Sixty-four Turkish-speaking parent-child dyads (32 girls, Mage = 26.1 months, SD = 1.33, 25 PT) were observed in free-play sessions. The form (i.e., WH, yes/no) and function (i.e., pedagogical, information-seeking, rhetorical) of parental questions and gestures accompanying them were coded. Children's working memory and cognitive flexibility skills were measured using Hide the Pots and Reverse Categorization (pre- and post-switch) tasks, respectively. Results showed that PT and FT children had similar EF skills. Parental WH questions were associated with PT children's working memory skills. Parental WH questions, not pedagogical ones, were related to children's cognitive flexibility skills, regardless of neonatal status. When accompanied by gestures, both WH and pedagogical questions were associated with PT children's working memory and cognitive flexibility skills. These results highlight the importance of specific parental input as a function of children's neonatal status in the development of EFs.

title: Early self-regulation in context: Multidimensional organization of neonatal non-nutritive sucking and its association with subclinical maternal depressive traits.
authors: Faré O, Silvestri V, Morniroli D, Petrelli A, Colombo L, Giannì ML, Bulf H
abstract: From the very first days of life, infants' affective regulation unfolds within a dyadic co-regulatory system shaped by caregiver responsivity. In contexts of reduced maternal availability, such as maternal depressive states, infants may be required to compensate for diminished interpersonal regulation by increasingly relying on their internal resources. Neonatal non-nutritive sucking (NNS) represents one of the earliest spontaneously available regulatory behaviors, contributing to physiological and behavioral homeostasis from birth. However, it remains unclear whether its spontaneous organization is associated with early relational vulnerability indexed by maternal depressive symptoms. The present study aimed to characterize the spontaneous organization of NNS in a sample of newborns (N = 42) and to examine whether individual differences in NNS are associated with maternal postnatal depressive subclinical traits measured using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). Results from an exploratory principal component analysis indicated that neonatal sucking behavior was organized along two functional dimensions, reflecting overall sucking effort and behavioral activation, and the temporal organization of sucking bursts. Importantly, higher maternal depressive traits, though subclinical, were selectively associated with increased sucking effort, with infants of mothers reporting higher depressive traits showing more frequent and intense sucking, while no differences emerged for the organizational dimension. Overall, these findings suggest that individual differences in maternal depressive traits within the subclinical range may be associated with neonatal NNS effort, a precocious compensatory mobilization of regulatory resources, potentially serving both to support autonomous regulation and to elicit maternal engagement.

title: Accuracy of parent and teacher reports of early math skills.
authors: King YA, Zippert EL, Ellis A, O'Rear C, Lin J, Purpura DJ
abstract: BACKGROUND: It is important for parents and teachers to understand preschooler's early mathematics skills to best provide appropriate mathematics support. Comparing parents' and teachers' accuracy in reporting children's mathematics skills may help to ensure developmentally appropriate early math support in home and classroom environments. AIM: The present study examined the accuracy of parents' and teachers' reports of preschoolers' early mathematics skills (i.e., counting, numeral identification, and quantitative and spatial word knowledge). SAMPLE: Participants included 117 children 3 to 5 years old (M = 4.27, SD = .63, 49.6 % female) and their parent and Head Start teacher. METHOD: Parents and teachers completed surveys reporting on each child's understanding of mathematics concepts via items from different mathematics measures. Children were directly assessed on their mathematics skills via the same or similar items. RESULTS: Generally, parents' and teachers' reports were positively associated with direct assessments of children's mathematics skills. Parents' and teachers' reports of children's mathematical skills ranged from 47 % to 75 % accurate, and parents were more accurate than teachers in reporting children's quantitative word knowledge. The direction of inaccuracies (over-or underestimation) varied by mathematics skill type, such that caregivers tended to overestimate children's numeracy skills and underestimate their mathematical language knowledge. CONCLUSION: Future research is needed to examine how the accuracy of parents and teachers reports influences early mathematics development, and how potentially improving caregiver accuracy might support children's mathematics learning.

title: Parent-child facial expression recognition: the role of familiarity in interactive contexts.
authors: Palmer K, Buttle HM, Kohler M, Fong FTK, Nelson NL
abstract: The ability to express and understand emotion is fundamental to social communication, and develops through early parent-child interactions. Across two studies, we examined parents' and children's recognition of emotional expressions during a structured interactive task. In Study 1, parent-child dyads (N = 33, children aged 4-9 years) took turns producing facial expressions in response to emotion-eliciting objects while their partner guessed the eliciting object. Videos of children were shown to naïve adult raters (N = 88) completing the same task. Study 1 provided initial evidence for a familiarity effect, with parents outperforming naïve raters at recognising their child's expressions. Study 2 (N = 45 dyads, children aged 4-12 years) extended this by testing whether recognition accuracy reflects familiarity with a specific partner or general parenting experience. Participants completed the task with each other and with videos of unfamiliar partners. Naïve parents (N = 69) and non-parents (N = 68) also rated the children's expressions. Study 2 confirmed a bidirectional familiarity advantage: both parents and children were more accurate with their familiar partner than with unfamiliar individuals, suggesting the effect is specific to the parent-child relationship rather than reflecting a general ability to read adult or child faces. Recognition accuracy was not strongly predicted by age, suggesting familiarity may account for more variance in performance than developmental changes in expressive clarity alone. These findings support the view that the unique parent-child bond plays a meaningful role in emotional understanding.

SVIP knockdown alters UPS protein expression in human testicular embryonal carcinoma cells.
authors: Kipel Ş, Çayli S, Aktaş Gİ, Nakkaş H
abstract: Testicular tumours are the most common malignant tumors in men between the ages of 15-34. Approximately 95% of testicular tumors arise from germ cells. Small VCP-interacting protein (SVIP) is a protein that regulates its function and autophagy by binding to p97/VCP, which is involved in protein degradation associated with the endoplasmic reticulum. Recent studies on SVIP have shown that SVIP is an androgen-sensitive protein. The development of secondary sex characteristics is influenced by androgens, which are significant steroid hormone. Androgens also initiate and maintain spermatogenesis in the male reproductive system. Mutations of androgen receptors are often seen in patients with disorders of male reproductive development and can cause male infertility. Studies are showing that the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS) in the male reproductive system affects fertility. Therefore, investigating the expressions of USP26 and UXT, which are components of the UPS, is important for testicular biology. The expressions of SVIP, AR, Ubiquitin, USP26 and UXT were analysed by immunofluorescence, western blot and q RT-PCR method to determine the expressions of SVIP and the UPS proteins that it interacts in human testicular embryonal carcinoma cells (CRL-2073) and to see the effects of suppressed SVIP expression on other proteins after SVIP siRNA transfection. At SVIP siRNA applied CRL-2073 cells, SVIP, AR, USP26 and Ubiquitin expressions decreased, while UXT expression increased, according to immunofluorescence and western blot results. According to the qRT-PCR results, SVIP gene expression decreased and AR, Ubiquitin, USP26 and UXT gene expressions increased in the group given SVIP siRNA. As a result, this study demonstrated the expression of SVIP and its interacting UPS proteins in CRL-2073 cells for the first time, making an unique and significant contribution to the literature.

title: Clinical characteristics and maternal whole-exome sequencing findings in patients with recurrent oocyte, zygote, and early embryo maturation arrest: a single-center experience.
authors: Kahraman S, Cetinkaya M, Cetinkaya CP, Madjunkova S, Kara B, Ayaz A, Aktoz F
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To characterize the clinical phenotype, cumulative assisted reproductive technology (ART) experience, and maternal whole-exome sequencing (WES) findings in patients with recurrent Oocyte, Zygote, and Early Embryo Maturation Arrest (OZEMA), and to assess the contribution of phenotype-guided genomic evaluation in this clinically challenging population. DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study conducted in a fertility clinic within a general private hospital equipped with an in‑house genetic laboratory. SUBJECTS: A total of 115 females with a history of OZEMA were included, all of whom presented to the ART clinic. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: The distribution of pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants in established OZEMA-associated genes, variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in established genes, monoallelic variants in established autosomal recessive genes, and exploratory candidate-gene findings. ART outcomes were described according to whether a prioritized WES finding was reported. RESULTS: The mean female age was 33.47 +/- 4.37 years, with a median infertility duration of 6.0 years (range, 1.0-21.0). Patients had experienced recurrent OZEMA across multiple ART cycles (median, 4; range, 1-16). Parental consanguinity was observed in 37 of 115 cases (32.2 %). Prioritized maternal WES findings were identified in 64 of 115 patients (55.7 %): 12 patients (10.4 %) had P/LP variants in established genes with genotypes consistent with the reported inheritance pattern, 17 (14.8 %) had VUS in established genes, 15 (13.0 %) had monoallelic variants in established autosomal recessive genes without a second relevant allele, and 20 (17.4 %) had exploratory candidate-gene findings. No prioritized WES finding was identified in 51 patients (44.3 %). CONCLUSIONS: Phenotype-guided maternal WES identified established P/LP findings with inheritance-consistent support in a clinically meaningful subset of patients with recurrent OZEMA and revealed a broader spectrum of additional genomic findings. These results support genomic evaluation, while the clinical interpretation of VUS, monoallelic findings in recessive genes, and exploratory candidate-gene findings should remain evidence-based.

Postoperative atrial fibrillation and use of oral anticoagulants after cardiac surgery: a real-life, single-centre study.
authors: Johannesson E, Erixon C, Thelaus L, Teurneau-Hermansson K, Sjögren J, Larsson M, Nozohoor S, Mörtsell D
abstract: UNLABELLED: Postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF) is the most common complication following cardiac surgery and is associated with significant morbidity. This study sought to provide a comprehensive and contemporary evaluation of the clinical course and management of POAF, with particular emphasis on the use of oral anticoagulants (OACs). DESIGN: This single-centre, retrospective, longitudinal study included patients undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass at Skåne University Hospital, Lund, between February 2020 and September 2021. Included patients had no prior history of atrial fibrillation (AF) or atrial flutter and survived to hospital discharge. Patients were excluded if they underwent redo surgery, heart transplantation, hypothermic circulatory arrest or had endocarditis. Data on POAF and OAC use were obtained through retrospective chart review. RESULTS: 1,012 patients were included, of whom 43% developed POAF. Among POAF patients, 8.8% were discharged with ongoing AF. OACs were prescribed to 38% of POAF patients at hospital discharge, with 31% of prescriptions initiated by a cardiothoracic surgeon. The cumulative incidence of documented AF was 7.9% at 3-month follow-up and 8.8% at 1 year. However, 89% of POAF patients remained on OAC therapy at 1-year follow-up, despite the low rates of documented AF recurrence. CONCLUSIONS: POAF is frequently observed after cardiac surgery but typically resolves during the early postoperative period. Nonetheless, a substantial proportion of patients were prescribed and remained on long-term OAC therapy despite an absence of documented AF at follow-up and the heightened bleeding risk of this population.

title: Hemodynamic effects of ventilating or not, during cardiopulmonary bypass in a porcine model.
authors: Kvalheim VL, Mongstad A, Husby P, Stangeland L, Nginamau ES, Osman TA, Yamada S, Grong K
abstract: Background. Optimal ventilator setting during cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) is unknown. Improved gas exchange and lung compliance have been suggested as favourable outcomes when lungs are ventilated. However, long-time effects have been hard to demonstrate. There has been less focus on the immediate circulatory effects of ventilator settings during cardioplegia and CPB, and potentially hemodynamic effects of different ventilator strategies are unknown. Methods. Sixteen anesthetized pigs on normothermic CPB with 80 min of aortic cross-clamp and cardioplegic arrest were randomized to a ventilated and a not ventilated group. After weaning, both cardiac-, hemodynamic-, and pulmonary functions were evaluated for up to 120 min. Results. Left ventricular variables and cardiac output did not differ between the two study groups, neither before nor after weaning. After weaning, mean pulmonary artery pressure was increased in ventilated compared to not ventilated animals. Neither pulmonary compliance nor oxygen uptake differed between groups in surviving animals. Conclusions. Disconnection of the ventilator during CPB and cardiac arrest did not affect lung compliance and oxygen uptake, neither positively nor negatively. In the ventilated group, a temporary increase in the pulmonary pressure after weaning was observed.

title: Multiple Rectal Neuroendocrine Tumors Treated by Endoscopic Resection: A Case Report.
authors: Matsuki H, Ichijima R, Sekiguchi M, Toyoshima N, Kawamura R, Mizuguchi Y, Takamaru H, Yamada M
abstract: Rectal neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) are typically solitary, and the occurrence of multiple lesions is uncommon. We present a case of multiple rectal NETs in a 41-year-old man. Colonoscopy performed at another hospital revealed three lesions (4 mm in the sigmoid colon and 5 and 10 mm in the rectum), all of which were diagnosed as NET, grade 1 (G1), following endoscopic resection; one lesion had a positive vertical margin. Upon referral to our institution, repeat colonoscopy demonstrated multiple yellowish, slightly elevated lesions throughout the rectum, all of which were histologically confirmed as NETs. Imaging studies showed no evidence of lymph node or distant metastasis. Although additional surgical resection was considered because of the multiplicity of lesions and positive margin, the patient strongly preferred endoscopic therapy. Eight lesions were successfully resected using endoscopic mucosal resection with a cap or endoscopic submucosal dissection. Histopathological examination revealed seven NET, G1 lesions and one NET, G2 lesion. Additional surgery was recommended but was declined by the patient, and no local recurrence or distant metastasis has been observed during 18 months of follow-up. This rare case highlights the potential role and the limitations of endoscopic treatment in patients with multiple rectal NETs.

title: Special Collection: Abstracts from IUNS-ICN Paris 2025
Limbic circuit alterations in bipolar disorder.
authors: Magioncalda P, Yeh CH, Lin HY, Tseng RY, Dabiri E, Conio B, Amore M, Mangin JF
abstract: INTRODUCTION: This study investigated the spatial and temporal pattern of brain white matter (WM) alterations and their relationship with intrinsic brain activity in bipolar disorder (BD). METHODS: Multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data were collected from 67 BD patients (during manic, depressive, or euthymic phases) and 125 healthy controls (HC) at baseline, and from a subsample of 33 BD patients (in a different illness phase) and 23 HC after follow-up. Analyses of diffusion MRI and resting-state functional MRI were performed to characterise fixel-based metrics in WM and their relationship with intrinsic brain activity in BD and HC, as well as across timepoints. RESULTS: BD exhibited a spatial pattern of WM alterations characterised by reductions in fibre density and/or bundle cross-section involving fornix and cingulum (major limbic pathways), alongside portions of other tracts, compared with HC. Reduced fibre density in the fornix was associated with intrinsic activity changes involving midbrain, thalamus, and connected fronto-temporal cortical areas within the default-mode network in BD. These alterations showed no significant changes over time or across illness phases. CONCLUSIONS: These findings converge on limbic circuit alterations and suggest a relationship between structural abnormalities of the fornix and functional changes in intrinsic brain architecture in BD.

title: Cortical spreading depression on Riemannian 2-manifolds: eikonal-curvature analysis and sulcal trapping.
authors: Enver A, Tepe N, Sara MY, Dilekoz E, Bolay H
abstract: Cortical spreading depression (CSD) is a slowly propagating wave of near-complete neuronal depolarization underlying migraine aura and implicated in stroke, traumatic brain injury, and subarachnoid hemorrhage. Existing reaction-diffusion models of CSD treat the cortex as a flat Euclidean domain, ignoring its highly folded, individually variable geometry. We develop a fully covariant FitzHugh-Nagumo (FHN) reaction-diffusion system on a smooth compact Riemannian 2-manifold [Formula: see text] representing the cortical sheet, in which the Euclidean Laplacian is replaced by the Laplace-Beltrami operator [Formula: see text]. Three mathematical results are established: (i) local and global well-posedness in [Formula: see text] together with positive invariance of the physiological region via parabolic semigroup theory; (ii) a curvature-corrected eikonal relation [Formula: see text], in which the wavefront speed is modulated by the geodesic curvature of the front; and (iii) a sulcal-trapping theorem giving an explicit criterion under which an excitable wave entering a sulcus (negative Gauss curvature region) remains confined to it. Numerically, we develop two complementary solvers: a discrete exterior calculus (DEC) scheme on triangulated surfaces using the cotangent Laplacian with implicit-explicit (IMEX) time-stepping, and a physics-informed neural network (PINN) surrogate that evaluates [Formula: see text] via the closest-point projection of the ambient Euclidean Laplacian. The PINN framework supports both forward simulation and the inverse identification of excitability fields from sparse observations, and a noise-ablation study quantifies its practical identifiability. The parameters of the slow subsystem and of the coupling functions are inherited from our published, cohort-calibrated thalamocortical model, which was calibrated against 67 paired-pulse somatosensory evoked potential (SEP) recordings from nine analysable animals of a cohort of 14 male Wistar rats (1, 233 sweeps) acquired in the Neuroscience Laboratory of Gazi University, with CSD induced by topical KCl application. We validate convergence on [Formula: see text] with the spectral ground-truth [Formula: see text], exhibit a propagating ring wave with a refractory tail, and verify the eikonal-curvature prediction across two orders of magnitude in geodesic curvature, including the leading correction due to the recovery variable; a mesh-convergence study yields explicit resolution requirements for evaluating the trapping criterion on MRI-derived cortical surfaces.

title: Ground-truth benchmarking of signed, directed lagged connectivity: TemporalSignedMBB from a simulated gut-br​ain model to neural data.
authors: Purboyo TW
abstract: Methods inferring signed, directed, window-specific connectivity are rarely tested against a known answer. We benchmarked TemporalSignedMBB, which combines Gaussian conditional transfer entropy, tracking of edge-sign transitions, persistent homology and a Laplacian perturbation score, against planted ground truth: independent replications of a gut-brain model of depression, an inferential null, seven misspecified generators, heterogeneous subject-specific couplings and a Wilson-Cowan neural-mass model. Under correct latent specification, transfer entropy recovered planted directed couplings with precision 0.91 and recall 0.67 to 0.91; detected edges had correct signs in over 99.9% of cases. A cluster-robust edge test was calibrated under the null, but the realized false discovery rate was 0.09 at nominal 0.05, owing to subject-demeaning bias in short panels. Sign tracking detected 76% of true reversals with 5 false reversals in 180 network comparisons. Lag mismatch, saturating or abundance-scale coupling and latent drivers lowered recall to 0.46 or raised false discoveries to 0.19. Persistent homology missed planted directed loops that a directed cycle count detected, and the perturbation score did not predict perturbation responses. Individual networks recovered subject-specific couplings poorly, and with matched learners, network features gave case-control AUROCs of 0.56 to 0.59, against 0.97 to 0.98 for abundance features exploiting planted mean shifts, and 0.56 to 0.58 when groups differed only in coupling. In the neural-mass model, excitatory and inhibitory signs were recovered with an adequate lag order but not under volume conduction or hemodynamic observation. The results support group-level transfer entropy and sign tracking under favorable conditions, not the complete framework.

title: Hydrogen-rich saline alleviates inflammation-associated depression-like behaviors in mice.
authors: Fu ZJ, Ren ZY, He L, Zhang L, Wang Y
abstract: Despite the crucial role of inflammation in depression-like behavior, the low blood-brain barrier penetration of existing anti-inflammatory agents presents a substantial obstacle to effective treatment. Owing to the excellent blood-brain barrier permeability and anti-inflammatory ability of hydrogen-rich saline, this study explores its therapeutic effects on lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation-associated depression-like behavior in mice. In this study, mice intraperitoneally received lipopolysaccharide (0.83 mg/kg). Thirty minutes later, they intraperitoneally received hydrogen-rich saline (5 mL/kg). Results showed that hydrogen-rich saline significantly alleviated anxiety- and depression-like behaviors in lipopolysaccharide-treated mice, as assessed by open field tests, elevated plus maze tests, forced swim tests, and the tail suspension test. Peripheral inflammation was significantly reduced, associated with inhibited splenomegaly and decreased serum levels of interleukin-1β and tumor necrosis factor-α. Central inflammation was also decreased, related to the reduced number of activated microglia, inhibition of Tolllike receptor 4/myeloid differentiation primary response 88/nuclear factor-κB signaling, and repaired synaptic damage in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that early hydrogen-rich saline administration may attenuate lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation-associated depression-like behaviors, at least in part, by suppressing microglial pro-inflammatory activation and Tolllike receptor 4/nuclear factor-κB signaling.

title: Sleep disturbance and enhanced aggression after chronic mild stress in mice: Association with hypothalamic nerve growth factor.
authors: Chikahisa S, Shiuchi T, Chiba S, Murata T, Séi H
abstract: Chronic stress disrupts sleep and induces behavioural abnormalities. However, the mechanisms linking stress-related sleep disturbances to abnormal social behaviour are unclear. In this study, a predictable chronic mild stress (CMS) paradigm was used, in which male mice were housed on a wire mesh for 3 weeks. CMS mice (n = 7 per group) had reduced non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and NREM slow-wave activity, and they had enhanced aggressive behaviour, whereas anxiety- and depression-related behavioural measures were not markedly altered. At the molecular level, CMS was associated with lower hypothalamic Ngf mRNA levels, and hypothalamic NGF protein levels were related to aggressive behaviour. Intracerebroventricular administration of NGF promoted sleep in control and CMS mice (n = 6-7 per group), but aggressive behaviour was suppressed only in CMS mice (n = 8 per group). These findings suggest that hypothalamic NGF may contribute to mechanisms that link chronic stress-related sleep disturbances with aggressive behaviour, although the precise downstream mechanisms are not known.

title: Time-dependent changes in auditory fear generalization and its suppression by extinction in mice.
authors: Dong X, Wang Y, Liu Y, Li Y
abstract: Fear responses often generalize from threat cues to perceptually similar stimuli, and excessive generalization is implicated in anxiety-related disorders. Although contextual fear generalization can increase over time, whether auditory fear generalization gradients change after conditioning remains unclear. Here we used an auditory fear-conditioning paradigm in male C57BL/6 J mice to examine time-dependent changes in tone generalization and whether CS-only extinction suppresses generalized fear. Mice received five tone-shock pairings at one of four shock intensities (0, 0.25, 0.4, or 1.0 mA). Generalization was assessed using the conditioned stimulus (CS; 6 kHz) and three lower-frequency generalization stimuli (GSs; GS1 3.8 kHz, GS2 3.0 kHz, GS3 2.4 kHz). To avoid repeated generalization testing before extinction, generalization at 24 h and 15 days after conditioning was assessed in independent cohorts. At 24 h, the 0.4 and 1.0 mA groups showed CS-biased gradients, with higher freezing to the CS than to the more distant GSs. At Day 15, freezing remained high but CS-GS discrimination was reduced; this was most evident in the 0.4 mA group, which showed a significantly shallower subject-level slope than the corresponding 24-h group. Two sessions of CS-only extinction reduced freezing to both the CS and untrained GSs, consistent with suppression of generalized auditory fear. These findings suggest that auditory fear generalization can become less stimulus-specific over time and that extinction can suppress generalized fear responses.

title: β-Caryophyllene, a CB2 receptor agonist improves stress-related behaviors and neurochemical alterations in a murine PTSD-like model.
authors: Hidalgo-Ayala LM, Espinoza-Gutiérrez HA, Flores-Soto ME, Tejeda-Martínez AR, Guzmán-Flores JM, Viveros-Paredes JM
abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterized by excessive fear, hypervigilance, and dysregulation of stress-response systems, notably the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) and sympathetic-adrenal-medullary (SAM) axes. Although benzodiazepines remain the most prescribed pharmacological treatment, their long-term use is associated with cognitive decline and fatigue, prompting the search for alternative therapeutic strategies. The endocannabinoid system (ECS) is a lipid-based neuro-immunomodulatory signaling network implicated in stress regulation. While the anxiolytic effects of cannabinoid type 1 (CB1) receptor agonism have been extensively examined, the potential role of cannabinoid type 2 (CB2) receptor activation remains largely unexplored. β-Caryophyllene is a naturally occurring dietary sesquiterpene and selective CB2 agonist. This study evaluated the effect of β-Caryophyllene on a murine PTSD-like model induced by a dual model of electric shock and acoustic stress in male C57BL/6 mice. β-Caryophyllene (10 mg / kg, oral) was administered either during or after stress exposure. The CB2 antagonist AM630 (2 mg / kg, intraperitoneal) was used to determine receptor involvement. Behavioral parameters were assessed using the light-dark box, open field, and elevated plus maze tests. Serum adrenaline, and serotonin were determined as part of the Sympathetic-Adrenal-Medullary axis activation, as well as corticosterone and central levels of glutamate as part of the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal axis activation. β-Caryophyllene improved anxiety- and compulsive-like behaviors, reduced amygdalar and hypothalamic glutamate concentrations and mitigated plasma corticosterone, and serotonin levels. These effects were reversed by AM630. Collectively, these findings suggest that the anxiolytic effect of β-Caryophyllene involves CB2, highlighting its therapeutic potential for PTSD.

title: SLC7A2 regulates the inflammation and apoptosis of LPS-induced human lung epithelial cells through TLR4/NF-κB pathway.
authors: Li X, Peng Y, Yin X
abstract: Acute lung injury (ALI) is the most common complication of sepsis and has a high mortality rate among critically ill patients. Its effective treatment still faces huge challenges. SLC7A2, an arginine transporter, is associated with immunity and inflammatory response. However, the action with specific regulation mechanism of SLC7A2 in LPS-treated ALI remains unclear. The key differentially expressed genes (DEGs) related to sepsis-associated ALI were screened out using the data from the GEO database. The interactions of DEGs were analyzed using bioinformatics analysis methods, such as GO, KEGG along with PPI networks. The LPS-treated human lung epithelial cells BEAS-2 B (HLECs-B) damage model was constructed. The mRNA or protein expression in LPS-treated HLECs-B were evaluated through application of RT-qPCR or western blot. CCK-8, EdU, TUNEL staining assay along with ELISA were applied to assess cells viability, proliferation, apoptosis, and inflammatory factors expression, respectively. Bioinformatics analysis of GEO datasets identified the top three DEGs (SLC7A2, TNIP3, and CFB). The mRNA levels of these 3 DEGs were highly raised in LPS-treated HLECs-B, and especially of SLC7A2. Functionally, in LPS-treated HLECs-B, SLC7A2 silencing could improve cell viability and proliferation, block apoptosis, reduce IL-1β, IL-6, along with TNF-α production; Moreover, SLC7A2 silencing could decrease the TLR4, p-NF-κB protein levels. Importantly, overexpression of TLR4 reversed the protective effects of SLC7A2 silencing, whereas knockdown of TLR4 abrogated the detrimental effects of SLC7A2 overexpression, in LPS-treated HLECs-B. SLC7A2 regulates the inflammation and apoptosis of LPS-treated lung epithelial cells through TLR4/NF-κB pathway.
